topic: America Imported Asian Carp to Clean Its Fish Ponds and Now They Rule the Mississippi
research_summary: Asian carp (silver, bighead, grass, and black carp) were deliberately imported into the United States in the 1960s and 1970s for aquaculture, water-quality/algae control, weed and snail control, and human food. Grass carp was the first, imported by the US Fish and Wildlife Service in 1963; bighead and silver carp were imported from China in 1973, initially to Arkansas. The earliest escapes are now attributed primarily to public-sector research and stocking programs rather than the 1990s floods often cited in media, though flooding did spread the fish. They escaped confinement, established reproducing populations across the Mississippi River Basin, and now occupy large portions of America's interior rivers, with at least one species established in 45 states. Silver carp are notorious for leaping up to ~10 feet when startled by boat motors, injuring boaters. The US Army Corps of Engineers built electric dispersal barriers on the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal (first operational 2002) and is constructing the ~$1.1 billion Brandon Road Interbasin Project to keep carp out of the Great Lakes. Comparable cases of introduced species that escaped control and devastated ecosystems include the cane toad in Australia (introduced 1935 to control cane beetles, a famous biocontrol failure) and the Nile perch in Lake Victoria (introduced 1950s-60s to boost fisheries, driving hundreds of endemic cichlid species toward extinction). The ledger was deliberately overbuilt to 56 claims to survive expected attrition from paywalls and unverifiable quotes, strongly favoring open-access USGS, FWS, university, DOI, and open-access journal pages.
